facts.claim: Logan Halstead wrote "Dark Black Coal" when he was 15. It was the first song he wrote and released.
The album Dark Black Coal was produced by Lawrence Rothman and recorded at Sound Emporium. It was released May 5, 2023 on Logan Halstead Records and distributed by Thirty Tigers.
Halstead played much of the guitar on the album himself.

The song went viral in December 2020 when RadioWV posted a video of it. Halstead recorded "Dark Black Coal" and "Far From Here" for RadioWV on the same day. He had written it earlier and had nearly forgotten it.
Halstead released a studio version of the viral song ahead of the album. Saving Country Music noted that comparisons to Tyler Childers followed the viral video.
Halstead said he wrote the song from his experience growing up in coal country. He described feeling trapped, with a love/hate relationship with the mines.
Halstead called it the first song he was ever proud of. He said he thought of the sacrifices his family and many others made for coal.
Halstead said his dad, uncle, grandfather and most of the men in his family worked in the mines around Boone County.
Halstead said he realized music could be a career when he saw the support for "Dark Black Coal" and people offered to pay to see him play. Before that, music was a hobby.
Halstead was born in Kentucky and raised in West Virginia. The song is the title track of his debut full-length album, released when he was 19.

draft:
The guitar on **Dark Black Coal** is fingerpicked and patient, with a steady bass line rolling under the melody. It's recorded close and dry, the kind of sound that puts you in a small room with whoever's playing. There are no harmonies, no other voices. When the singing arrives it's low and a little gravelly, and the tempo stays slow and unhurried. Nothing is dressed up.

That plainness suits where the song comes from. Logan Halstead wrote it at 15, in Boone County, West Virginia, where his dad, his uncle, his grandfather, and most of the men in his family worked the mines. He has said he wrote it out of growing up in coal country, out of feeling trapped there and holding a love/hate relationship with the mines. That's a complicated thing for a teenager to carry. The mines are what fed his family, and they're also the walls around his future. He also called it the first song he was ever proud of, and he said he was thinking about the sacrifices his family and many others made for coal.

So two feelings sit together in this song and neither cancels the other. One is the urge to get out. The other is gratitude, maybe even reverence, for the people who stayed and gave their bodies to the work. Halstead doesn't have to pick one, and the spare arrangement doesn't make him. A bigger production might have tipped the song toward anthem or toward lament. This one just leaves a guitar and a voice to hold both.

The song's own story has a turn in it, too. Halstead had nearly forgotten it by the time he cut it for RadioWV, on the same day he recorded "Far From Here." The video went viral in December 2020, and the Tyler Childers comparisons followed fast. Halstead has said that seeing that support, and people offering to pay to see him play, was when he realized music could be a career instead of a hobby. A song about feeling stuck in coal country turned out to be his way forward.

It sits squarely in the Appalachian coal-country songwriting tradition, a line that runs through Childers and Arlo McKinley, who guests on the album. The studio version became the title track of Halstead's debut, produced by Lawrence Rothman at Sound Emporium and released when he was 19. He played much of the record's guitar himself, and the song keeps the bare, close feel of someone working through his own history.

What sticks is how the song lets you love a place and need to leave it in the same breath, without asking you to feel guilty about either.
